# The Thread — retry v2 (blind-pass generation, 2026-08-06)

**Generated by**: `skills/mark-forsyth-rhetoric/workflows/04-write-to-enchant.md`, pure Forsyth, single author.
**Retry rationale** (per `directives/embodiment-standard.md` — one retry against the weakest checklist item):
v1 failed the recognition test on the close. It ended on an earnest instruction ("Your reader is that man.
Give them something to hold") where Forsyth ends on a joke; it also carried far fewer stacked examples than

---

I cannot follow a plot. I lose the thread.

I say that without thinking, and so do you, and neither of us has ever asked what thread we mean, or who was
holding the other end of it, or why it has not been tidied away by now along with the rest of the wool.

Because it is wool. That is the whole point.

A clue used to be a *clew*, and a clew was a ball of yarn. Nothing else. If you had wound your wool into a
sphere you had made a clew, and there was no detective anywhere near it. The Oxford English Dictionary is
perfectly calm about this: the ball of thread comes first, and everything glamorous happens afterwards.

What happened afterwards was Theseus.

You know the arrangement. There is a labyrinth, there is a Minotaur in the middle of it, and there is the
inconvenient detail that killing the Minotaur is only half a plan, because the other half is getting out
again. Ariadne — far and away the most competent person in the story — hands him a ball of wool. He ties one
end to the door, unwinds it as he goes, kills his monster, picks up the thread and walks home.

He followed the clew. And that story was retold so often, and by so many people, that the word for the wool
became the word for the thing that gets you out of a maze, and then the word for any small hint that gets
you out of any muddle whatsoever, until eventually a clue is a cigarette end in a flowerbed and has not been
made of wool since about the time of the Armada.

The metaphor was never actually retired, though. It was only forgotten, which is not the same thing and is
much more fun. We still lose the thread. We follow a line of argument, we tie up loose ends, we spin a yarn,
we get tangled, we tease a problem apart, we string somebody along, we are given the runaround by a shaggy
dog story, and a plot — the language being almost insultingly obvious here — is a thing you *unwind*.

Which raises a small professional point, and then I shall stop.

When a reader tells you they got lost in something you wrote, you will assume they mean it was too
difficult. They almost never mean that. People read appallingly difficult things quite happily and always
have; the Globe was full of illiterates having a marvellous time. What they mean is that you dropped the
wool. Somewhere around the third paragraph you stopped tying each sentence to the one in front of it, and
the reader, who had been holding on very loyally until then, discovered there was nothing in their hand.

So the cure is not to simplify. Simplifying a piece that has lost its thread gives you something thin *and*
still baffling, which is the worst result available to anybody. The cure is to walk back to the last place
the reader was definitely still with you — always earlier than you would like — and pay the wool out again
from there.

Ariadne's gift, you will notice, was not the wool. Anyone can produce wool. Her gift was noticing that the
man going into the maze and the man coming out of it were in rather different conditions, and that only one
of them was in any state to be clever about left turns.

She was, in the terminology, a give-clew. I accept that this has not caught on.
